questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT a correct statement about class variables?
options: They are defined inside a class definition, but not inside a method definition.
They can be accessed using a class object.
They can have any type.
They are immutable.
rationales: It is true that class variables are defined inside a class definition, but not inside a method definition.
It is true that class variables can be accessed using a class object.
It is true that class variables can have any type.
This statement is false -- that is, class variables are mutable.

questions.question_text:
Suppose we define a `Card` class like this:

```
class Card:

    def __init__(self, suit, rank):
        self.suit = suit
        self.rank = rank
```

If this class does not provide an `__eq__` method, what happens if we compare two cards using the `==` operator?
options: That's an error.
By default, only the first attribute is compared.
By default, all of the attributes are compared as if they were in a tuple.
By default, the objects are equal only if they are identical.
rationales: It is not an error -- if a class provides no `__eq__`, the `==` operator has a default behavior.
If a class provides no `__eq__`, the `==` operator checks whether objects are identical.
If a class provides no `__eq__`, the `==` operator checks whether objects are identical.
If a class provides no `__eq__`, the `==` operator checks whether objects are identical.

questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements is true when one class inherits from another, like this:

```
class Hand(Deck):
    """Represents a hand of playing cards."""
```
options: `Hand` is a parent class and `Deck` is a child class.
Every function that works with `Hand` should also work with `Deck`.
Every `Hand` object has the same attributes as every `Deck` object, no more or less.
Every method defined in the `Deck` class can also be invoked on a `Hand` object.
rationales: In this example, `Hand` inherits from `Deck`, so `Hand` is the child class and `Deck` is the parent.
If `Hand` inherits from `Deck`, it could have additional methods that don't work with `Deck`.
If `Hand` inherits from `Deck`, a `Hand` object should have all of the attributes of a `Deck` object, but it can have more.
If `Hand` inherits from `Deck`, every method defined in the `Deck` class should work with a `Hand` object.

questions.question_text: What do we call it when one method invokes another to do most or all of the work?
options: inheritance
generalization
specialization
delegation
rationales: Inheritance is the ability to define a new class that is a modified version of a previously defined class.
Generalization is when we add a parameter to a function to make its capabilities more general.
Specialization is a way of using inheritance to create a new class that is a specialized version of an existing class.
Delegation is when one method passes responsibility to another method to do most or all of the work.

questions.question_text:
The `Hand` class in this chapter inherits from `Deck` and defines its own `__init__`:

```
class Hand(Deck):
    def __init__(self, label=''):
        self.label = label
        self.cards = []
```

When we create a `Hand` with `Hand('player 1')`, which `__init__` methods run?
options: `Deck.__init__` runs first, then `Hand.__init__`.
Only `Deck.__init__` runs, because `Hand` inherits it.
Neither -- it's an error, because `Deck.__init__` requires a `cards` argument.
Only `Hand.__init__`, which overrides `Deck.__init__`, so it has to create all the attributes a `Hand` needs.
rationales: Python doesn't run the parent's `__init__` automatically -- if the child class defines `__init__`, only the child's version runs.
`Hand` would inherit `Deck.__init__` only if it didn't define its own; because it does, its version overrides the one in `Deck`.
`Deck.__init__` is never called, so its parameters don't matter -- `Hand('player 1')` works and the `Hand` gets the label `'player 1'`.
`Hand.__init__` overrides `Deck.__init__`, so `Deck.__init__` doesn't run -- that's why `Hand.__init__` creates the `cards` attribute itself.
